results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Explained: On-Demand, Reserved, Bare Metal
highlights:
GPU cloud pricing looks simple on a rate card, but the hourly number hides two separate decisions: How you commit to paying for capacity, and how much of the server you actually get. Understanding both is what separates a GPU bill that tracks useful work from one that pays for idle hardware.

- On-demand buys flexibility: You pay per GPU-hour with no commitment and can stop at any time, which suits experiments, bursty jobs, and workloads whose utilization you have not measured yet.
- Reserved pricing buys a lower rate: Committing to a term lowers the effective hourly price, but you pay for every hour of the term, so it only saves money when utilization stays above the break-even point set by the discount.
- Bare metal is a deployment model, not a billing term: It gives you the whole physical server with root access and no hypervisor, which can be bought on demand or reserved, and NVIDIA has measured virtualized training running 12% slower than bare metal.
- Published rates are only a starting point: On GMI Cloud, on-demand rates start at $2.60 per GPU-hour for H100, $3.20 for H200, $5.00 for B200, and $8.00 for GB200 as of October 2026, while committed plans are discounted and storage and networking are priced separately.
- Utilization decides which model wins: Cast AI’s 2026 analysis of production clusters found average enterprise GPU utilization of roughly 5%, which shows how easily reserved capacity turns into paid idle time. Matching the pricing model to measured usage is the single biggest lever on GPU cost.

...

Every GPU cloud quote answers two separate questions. The first is the billing term: Do you pay as you go, or do you commit to a period in exchange for a lower rate? The second is the deployment model: Do you get a container on shared infrastructure, a virtual machine, a whole physical server, or a managed cluster? On-demand and reserved are answers to the first question. Bare metal is an answer to the second. That is why the same bare metal server can be rented on demand for a test and reserved for a year of training.

| | On-demand (pay as you go) | Reserved (committed term) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container or VM | Fast start, no commitment, highest hourly rate | Lower rate for a fixed term, paid whether used or not |
| Bare metal server | Full server control for short or uncertain workloads | Full server control at the lowest effective rate for steady, long-running work |

...

On-demand pricing charges a rate per GPU-hour while your instance is running, with no minimum term. You can start, scale, and stop whenever you like, and the bill follows usage, provided you actually release capacity when it is idle. Metering granularity matters for short jobs. Some providers bill by the second or minute, others round up to the hour, and that difference adds up quickly for bursty work.

On GMI Cloud, all GPU resources are dedicated, single-tenant instances priced per GPU-hour, with the rate depending on GPU type and deployment model. Pay-as-you-go containers have no expiration date and can be terminated at any time, and pay-as-you-go managed clusters are charged by the minute with no upfront cost, as GMI explains in its guide to comparing container, bare metal, and managed cluster quotes.

...

### On-Demand GPU Rates on GMI Cloud

The table below shows GMI Cloud’s published starting rates, taken from the GMI Cloud pricing page in October 2026. Rates vary by region and deployment model and can change with promotions, so treat them as starting points and confirm the live rate in the GMI Cloud console before you budget.

| GPU | On-demand rate (October 2026) | Availability (October 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 | From $2.60 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA H200 | From $3.20 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA B200 | From $5.00 per GPU-hour | Limited availability |
| NVIDIA GB200 | From $8.00 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA GB300 | Pre-order | Pre-order |

## Reserved and Committed GPU Pricing

### How Reservations Work

Reserved pricing, also called committed-use pricing, trades flexibility for a lower effective rate. You commit to a GPU type, quantity, and term, and the provider prices that capacity below its on-demand rate. In exchange, you pay for the full term whether the GPUs are busy or idle, and you usually cannot cancel early.

On GMI Cloud, containers can run on prepaid plans with renewal periods from one day to three years, and a prepaid container cannot be terminated before its rental period ends. Committed usage plans are discounted relative to on-demand, with volume and custom pricing handled by the sales team. Before you confirm an order, the console shows the list price, the discount, and the estimated monthly total, which makes it easy to compare a committed plan with the on-demand equivalent.

...

Reservations no longer have to mean multi-year contracts. Many providers now sell short reservations sized for a single training run. AWS, for example, lets customers reserve GPU capacity through EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML with a start date up to eight weeks ahead and durations from one day up to 182 days. GMI Cloud’s prepaid terms starting at one day follow the same logic: Reserve exactly the window you need, then release it.

### The Utilization Break-Even

A reservation saves money only when you would otherwise have used the capacity for most of the term. The break-even point follows directly from the discount.

reserved is cheaper when expected utilization > (reserved rate ÷ on-demand rate)

With a 30% discount, the reserved rate is 70% of on-demand, so the reservation pays off only if you would have kept the GPUs running more than 70% of the time on demand. With a 50% discount, the break-even falls to 50%. A quick example makes the stakes concrete. Eight H100s running around the clock for a 730-hour month cost about $15,184 at GMI Cloud’s October 2026 on-demand rate of $2.60 per GPU-hour. If a committed plan priced that capacity 30% lower, it would cost about $10,629, which beats on-demand only if you would otherwise have run those eight GPUs for more than about 511 hours of the month.

...

A bare metal GPU server gives you the entire physical machine, typically eight GPUs with their CPUs, memory, local storage, and network adapters, with full root and operating system access and no hypervisor in between. On GMI Cloud, Bare Metal GPU includes custom drivers, persistent local NVMe, and hardware-level control to stop, start, reboot, or power-cycle the machine. It runs in an isolated VPC on RDMA-ready infrastructure, and GMI’s H200 servers are built with eight 400G NDR InfiniBand compute adapters for multi-node training.

...

Bare metal is priced per GPU-hour like other options, so its value shows up in throughput rather than in the rate itself. Removing the virtualization layer gives the workload direct access to GPUs, NVLink, and InfiniBand. In its Exemplar Cloud lessons, NVIDIA reported a case in which GB200 NVL72 FP8 pretraining ran 12% slower in a virtual machine than on bare metal. On a long training run, a 12% gap is effectively a 12% price difference, even at identical hourly rates. GMI Cloud has been recognized as an NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud for training on GB300 NVL72 systems, which means its infrastructure met NVIDIA’s performance thresholds against reference architecture.

...

## Spot and Serverless: Two Other Pricing Models

Two more models complete the picture. Spot or preemptible pricing sells unused capacity at a deep discount, up to 90% off on-demand on AWS, in exchange for the risk of interruption, which makes it suitable only for workloads that checkpoint and restart cleanly. Serverless inference removes GPU-hours from the bill altogether and charges per token or per request instead. GMI Cloud’s inference engine offers both per-token serverless APIs and dedicated endpoints, and per-token prices carry their own promotions. In October 2026, for example, the console listed DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 40% off, and a dedicated endpoint ran on one H200 at $4.50 per hour per replica.

## Costs That Sit Outside the GPU Rate

The GPU-hour rate usually covers compute only. On GMI Cloud, storage and networking are priced separately when you allocate them, and several of these line items can outweigh a small difference in GPU rates. Persistent storage is one, since container-local data does not survive reconfiguration and workloads that need durable data need a volume. Public IP addresses are another. GMI Cloud bills Elastic IPs by the minute on pay as you go, and they keep billing after they are disassociated until you release them, even when the container they served has been terminated.

Service levels belong in the comparison too. GMI Cloud’s service level agreement sets monthly availability for container instances at no less than 99% in a single region and 99.9% across multiple regions, with service credits based on affected GPUs and downtime hours. Bare metal availability commitments and credits are set in each order. When you compare providers, record any line a quote leaves out as not quoted rather than zero, then divide the full total by the units of work you care about, such as tokens served or training steps completed.

results.title: Every Term You Need to Understand AI Compute Pricing
results.author: DataStorage Editorial Team
highlights:
On October 10, 2026, eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs rented as a single node listed at $31.92 an hour on Lambda and $98.32 an hour on Microsoft Azure. Same silicon, same generation, a 3.1x gap. Run either for a month and the difference is $48,472 for one node.

...

For most of 2025 the story was simple: prices fell. AWS cut on-demand pricing on its H100-based P5 instances by 44 percent in June 2025 (AWS News Blog, 2025). That era is over. SemiAnalysis tracked one-year H100 contract pricing rising from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026, an increase of about 38 percent, as on-demand capacity sold out (SemiAnalysis, 2026). On October 1, 2026, Nebius raised on-demand H100 pricing from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour and B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, its second increase in a few months (Nebius pricing page, 2026; Stocktwits, 2026).

When prices move in both directions at once, falling on spot marketplaces and rising on contracts, the term attached to the number matters as much as the number itself. Note the source bias too: several widely cited price ranges come from GPU vendors with an interest in making their own rate look cheap. We use first-party price lists wherever possible and say so when we do not.

...

### Billing granularity

How finely usage is metered: per second, per minute, or per hour. AWS and Google Cloud bill GPU instances per second, Azure per minute, and some providers still round up to a full hour (GMI Cloud, 2026). For long training runs it barely matters. For bursty inference, evaluation jobs or agent sandboxes that spin up for 10 minutes at a time, hourly rounding can inflate effective cost several times over.

...

A published daily or weekly benchmark of rental rates for a specific chip.

...

- GPU prices are moving in both directions: spot marketplaces stay cheap while contract and neocloud on-demand rates rose through 2026, including Nebius's October 1 increase of up to 21 percent.
- Compare effective cost per useful GPU-hour, not list rate. Idle time can erase any provider discount.
- Compute futures on CME turn GPU rental into a hedgeable commodity. Plan AI budgets for commodity-style volatility.
- Keep training data on zero-egress storage so you can follow the cheapest available GPUs without paying to leave.

results.title: GMI Cloud Seeks $635M Loan Backed by GPU Contracts — Die Signal
results.author: Marcus Bennett
highlights:
GMI Cloud is seeking a $635m loan secured against customer contracts for GPU capacity, per Data Center Dynamics — a shift toward debt backed by AI compute commitments.

...

GMI Cloud is seeking a $635 million loan secured against customer contracts for GPU capacity, according to a report by Data Center Dynamics.

The figure is the story. Six hundred thirty-five million dollars, raised not against property or servers, but against signed commitments from customers who want GPU compute. That structure marks a shift in how AI infrastructure gets funded, and it deserves a close look at the mechanism.

...

A conventional data center loan leans on the building. Lenders take the land, shell, and power infrastructure as collateral. GMI Cloud's reported deal works differently. The collateral is contractual: agreements in which customers commit to paying for GPU capacity over time.

For the lender, this changes the risk profile. The loan's value depends on whether customers keep paying, not on real estate valuations. For the borrower, it unlocks capital without mortgaging physical assets directly.

Three elements drive the structure:

- Long-term customer commitments for GPU capacity
- Predictable revenue streams those contracts create
- A lender willing to price risk against contract quality rather than bricks

...

The report does not specify the lenders involved, the interest terms, or the contract durations underpinning the deal. Those details will determine whether the structure becomes a template or stays a one-off.

results.title: GMI Cloud funding: $223M Series B, $445M credit line
results.author: Hussein Mukhtar
highlights:
- 1 GMI Cloud raised a $223 million Series B led by ARCHIV, with Nvidia participating, announced on September 30, 2026.
- 2 A $445 million credit facility led by CTBC brings total new financing to $668 million, per Pulse 2.
- 3 The company plans data center expansion into the US and Japan and rents Nvidia H100, H200 and Vera Rubin GPUs.

...

GMI Cloud, a provider of on-demand graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity for artificial intelligence, announced on September 30, 2026, that it raised a $223 million Series B round led by ARCHIV, according to Pulse 2 and SiliconANGLE. GMI Cloud funding also includes a $445 million credit facility led by CTBC (ChinaTrust Commercial Bank), for $668 million in total, Pulse 2 reported. SiliconANGLE put the credit line at $440 million.

Nvidia (NVDA) took part in the equity round alongside DSC Investment, KT Corp., Kyobo Life, KB Investment and Trend Micro, according to both reports; SiliconANGLE also listed Redwood among the investors. Pulse 2 described ARCHIV as a San Francisco-based investment firm, and SiliconANGLE said it focuses on AI and robotics. Valuation was not disclosed in the coverage we reviewed.

GMI Cloud sells AI infrastructure as a service. Customers can rent Nvidia H100, H200 and Vera Rubin chips, and the company runs a Kubernetes-based Cluster Engine, its own software for allocating computing resources automatically. Kubernetes is a widely used open-source system for managing software containers across many servers.

The company operates data centers in Taiwan, Thailand and Malaysia and is expanding into the US and Japan, SiliconANGLE reported. Pulse 2, citing the company, described plans to add GPU capacity across the US, Taiwan and the Asia-Pacific region with an emphasis on Nvidia GB200 and GB300 NVL72 rack systems.

...

For companies buying AI compute, each well-funded neocloud is another place to source GPUs beyond Amazon, Microsoft and Google. Procurement teams negotiating training or inference capacity should get quotes from specialist providers like GMI Cloud and compare price per GPU-hour, contract length, and how quickly new chips such as Vera Rubin actually become available.

CFOs and boards should look closely at how these providers are financed. GMI Cloud's package leans heavily on debt: the credit facility is roughly twice the size of the equity round. Debt-funded GPU fleets depend on steady rental demand to service loans, so buyers signing multi-year commitments should ask about the provider's financial health, data center ownership and what happens to capacity if the lender's terms change.

results.title: Nvidia partner GMI Cloud calls CoreWeave’s 15% yield ‘insane’ - Moneyweb
results.author: Aileen Chuang, Bloomberg
highlights:
The founder of a cloud computing company with a similar business model to CoreWeave said the 15% yield on the latter’s bonds is “insane,” compared with the roughly 3.45% rate his company secured on a recent Taiwan dollar loan.

“This is an advantage,” GMI Cloud Chief Executive Officer Alex Yeh said in an interview on Thursday. He argued that cheaper capital and faster execution — helped by proximity to Asian supply chains — give AI infrastructure companies that operate in the region an edge as investor jitters raise funding costs for their Western rivals.

...

CoreWeave bonds this week were trading at deeply distressed levels, sparked by wariness of its plans to take on even more debt after already borrowing tens of billions to finance an unprecedented buildout of AI computing capacity. Meanwhile, companies like GMI Cloud benefit from being able to borrow in local currencies, which significantly lowers their costs compared with raising debt in dollars.

CoreWeave and GMI Cloud are so-called neoclouds, which sell computing power generated from advanced computer chips that are used to train AI. Their success is contingent on their graphics processing units coming online on schedule, because the companies have borrowed large sums of money against customer contracts that can only generate revenue once the projects are up and running.

...

These types of deals have grown rapidly in the US but are only beginning to take off in Asia, where GMI Cloud is among the few companies borrowing money to purchase GPUs. Last month, it secured a NT$13.9 billion ($429 million) five-year loan from 14 banks for a data centre in Taiwan. The company was also seeking another $300 million for a facility in Thailand, people familiar with the matter said earlier.

CoreWeave and GMI Cloud both have agreements with their supplier Nvidia Corp. to purchase unsold computing power, though the deals are structured differently. Such arrangements have raised concerns of circular financing that creates false demand. On Thursday, Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said his company didn’t need to backstop CoreWeave and that its cost of capital “is actually decreasing.”
